references.text: The immediate fulfillment of God's command in verse 24 – God makes the livestock, creeping things, and wild animals, each according to its kind.
God forms all the beasts of the field and birds of the heavens from the ground, which expands on the creation account from 1:24.
God's instructions to Noah to take pairs of every kind of animal into the ark reflect the same categories (livestock, creeping things, birds) as in the creation of 1:24.
The listing of wild animals, livestock, creeping things, and birds that entered the ark uses the same categories as the creation account in 1:24.
God's covenant with all living creatures after the flood reflects back to their original creation in 1:24.
A song of praise that honors God for the diversity of creation and His wisdom in filling the earth with living beings, mirroring the work of creation in 1:24.
An invitation to ask the animals and birds – they testify that God's hand has created all life, in line with the creation account in 1:24.
God declares that He has made the earth with humans and animals on it, pointing back to the creation of land animals in 1:24.
A direct parallel in the creation account showing the orderly progression from plants to animals, both using the expression 'each according to its kind'.
Restoration of the creation mandate: The animals created in 1:24 are now commanded to fill the earth again after the flood.
Complementary description: 1:24 creates the animals, while 1:30 establishes their ecological role and provision within the order of creation.
Structural parallel in the creation account: Both verses show the fulfillment of God's word that the earth should bring forth creatures 'each according to its kind'.
Contrast between creation and judgment: What was created to fill the earth in 1:24 is called to judgment in Isaiah 34.
Dramatic contrast: The animals created for life in 1:24 are called as a sacrifice in Ezekiel's prophecy of judgment.
Tragic contrast: The list of creatures in 1:24 becomes the object of God's regret and decision to destroy them in 6:7.
Development of the creation relationship: 1:24 establishes the existence of animals, while 9:2 defines their new relationship to humanity after the flood.
Perversion of creation: The beast in Revelation usurps God's role as the recipient of worship, in contrast to the creation account in 1:24.
Metaphorical use: The concept of beasts from 1:24 is used in Daniel as a symbol for a kingdom that will devour the earth.
Contrast between creation and judgment: Animals created in 1:24 are called to eat in a prophecy of destruction.
Theological development: 1:24 establishes the existence of animals, while 9:3 changes their role to becoming food for humanity.
Theological parallel: God's plan for restoration in Jeremiah reflects his original creative act in 1:24.
Theological parallel: The human mandate to fill the earth in 9:1 mirrors the original commission given to animals in 1:24.
Theological foundation: Isaiah uses the creation of the earth and animals (as in 1:24) as proof of God's sovereignty.
Theological parallel: The human mission to fill the earth in Acts 17 mirrors the original commission given to animals in 1:24.
Theological parallel: God's plan for restoration in Ezekiel reflects his original creative act in 1:24.
Direct reference: The psalm uses the list of creatures from 1:24 as a basis for praising the Creator.
Contrast between creation and judgment: Animals created to be good in 1:24 become objects of God's wrath in Jeremiah.
